title: Model Routing Is Simple. Until It Isn't.
hook: Picking the 'right' model per query looks like classification. IBM Research argues it's really a systems-optimization problem — and treating it as less costs money and speed.
key_points: True cost isn't just token pricing: Sonnet cost $0.19/task vs. GPT-4.1's $0.37/task on IBM's agent test, mostly from cheaper cache-read pricing.
Task difficulty is often invisible at routing time, and routers must juggle cost, latency, specialization, and compliance simultaneously.
Latency is frequently dominated by infrastructure — hardware, cache warmth, endpoint congestion — not raw model speed.
Their fix: treat routing as simultaneous optimization across cost/quality/latency, adding only ~6ms and 2KB of memory per decision.
On AppWorld with a CodeAct agent + Claude Sonnet, their router hit 84% accuracy for $93/83s — 21% cheaper, 9% faster than baseline, 4% less accurate.
content_html: Model routing sounds like a classification problem: look at a query, pick the model best suited to answer it. IBM Research argues that framing breaks down in practice, because the real drivers of cost, quality, and latency are entangled with the workload and the serving infrastructure in ways a simple classifier can't see.
extra_html: Three things complicate routing, per the post: actual cost depends on interactions like caching, not just sticker token prices — Claude Sonnet came in at roughly half GPT-4.1's per-task cost on their AppWorld test because agent workloads reuse context and Sonnet's cache-read pricing rewards that; task difficulty is often unknowable until a request is already executing, and routers must satisfy multiple constraints (cost, latency, specialization, compliance) simultaneously; and user-facing latency is often set by infrastructure overhead, not the model itself. IBM's response is to reframe routing as a lightweight systems-optimization problem across all three axes at once, adding only about 6ms and 2KB of memory per decision. On the AppWorld Test Challenge with a CodeAct agent and Claude Sonnet, their router reached 84% accuracy at $93 total cost and 83 seconds of latency — cheaper and faster than baseline for a modest accuracy tradeoff, and covering more of the cost/quality/latency frontier than a standard difficulty-based router. Full post on Hugging Face.

related.title: The Shadow Price of Reasoning
related.hook: When you can't afford to let every query think as long as it wants, who gets the compute? Treat reasoning tokens like a scarce resource and economics gives a clean answer.

related.title: Route the Task, Not the Call
related.hook: Agent quality only reveals itself at the end of a long workflow — so a router deciding per LLM call can never tell which decision earned the reward. Decide once, at admission.

flashcards.prompt: Why did Claude Sonnet cost less per task than GPT-4.1 in IBM's AppWorld test, despite similar-looking pricing?
flashcards.back_html: Agent workloads reuse context across steps, and Sonnet's cheaper cache-read pricing paid off disproportionately: $0.19/task vs. GPT-4.1's $0.37/task.

flashcards.prompt: Per IBM Research, why doesn't treating routing as difficulty-based classification work well?

choices.text: Difficulty is often invisible until execution starts, and routers must juggle cost, latency, specialization, and compliance at once
Classification models are too slow to run per request
All LLMs perform identically on difficult tasks

flashcards.explanation_html: A request that looks simple, like 'summarize,' can quietly trigger retrieval, compliance checks, and tool use, so difficulty alone can't drive routing.

flashcards.prompt: What's IBM Research's proposed reframing of model routing?
flashcards.back_html: Treat it as simultaneous optimization across cost, quality, and latency, not single-axis difficulty classification — at ~6ms and 2KB overhead per decision.

flashcards.prompt: How did IBM's systems-optimization router compare to baseline on AppWorld with a CodeAct agent + Claude Sonnet?

choices.text: 21% cheaper and 9% faster, for a 4% accuracy drop (84% accuracy)
Same cost and latency, but 20% more accurate
50% cheaper but roughly twice as slow

flashcards.explanation_html: The optimization-based router traded a small accuracy dip for a real cost and latency win, and covered more of the tradeoff space than a standard difficulty-based router.
